generalists-specialists-s1.title: Two bird species before and after a forest is cleared

table.caption: Number of breeding pairs in a 10 km² study area before and after most of its old forest was cleared for farms and houses (invented data for practice)

generalists-specialists-s2.title: Food sizes eaten by two species

items.q: Based on the table, which statement correctly classifies the two birds?
options: W is a specialist and X is a generalist
W is a generalist and X is a specialist
Both are specialists, because both eat insects
Both are generalists, because both live in forests

why.correct: Classify by how many foods, habitats and conditions a species can use.
options: Right: W uses one food and one nesting site; X uses many of each.
W eats one food type and nests in one kind of site, which is a narrow niche.
Bird X also eats seeds, fruit and scraps, a broad diet.
Living in a forest does not make a species a generalist; the range of resources it uses does.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in breeding pairs of woodpecker W after the clearing, then give the answer.

mistakes.why: That is the change in pairs. Divide by 40 and multiply by 100.
The size is right, but the pairs went down, so the percent change is negative: -85%.
Start from the value before clearing: (new - old) / old, so (6 - 40) / 40 × 100.
Divide by the starting value, 40 pairs, not by 6.

items.q: Which explanation best accounts for the change in woodpecker W?
options: Bird X ate most of the woodpecker’s eggs after clearing
Clearing removed the large dead trees it needs for both food and nests
The woodpecker moved to the new houses and was not counted
The woodpecker began eating seeds and scraps instead

why.correct: A specialist declines when the one resource it depends on is removed.
options: Nothing in the data shows predation by bird X.
Right: as a specialist, W had no other food or nest site to switch to.
W nests only in holes in large dead trees, not in buildings.
If it had switched foods, it would have done better, not worse.

items.q: By how many breeding pairs did bird X increase after the clearing?

mistakes.why: That adds the two counts. The increase is the difference: 65 - 50.
That is 30%, the percent change. The question asks for the number of pairs: 65 - 50.

items.q: Which feature of the figure shows that one species is a specialist?
options: Its curve is low and spread from 0 to 20 mm
Its curve crosses the other curve twice
Its curve is tall and narrow, centered on 6 mm food
Its curve starts at zero on the left side

why.correct: Niche width shows as the width of the curve.
options: A wide spread of food sizes is the mark of a generalist.
Crossing points do not show the width of a niche.
Right: it eats a narrow range of food sizes.
Both curves start low; the width of each curve is what matters.

items.q: A drought kills the plants that make 6 mm seeds, but seeds of other sizes remain. Which outcome does the figure predict?
options: The generalist declines more, because it eats more sizes
Both increase, because there is less competition for 6 mm seeds
Neither changes, because both can switch to 15 mm seeds
The specialist declines, while the generalist eats other sizes

why.correct: Losing the specialist’s main food hurts it most.
options: Eating more sizes lets the generalist switch, so it is hurt less.
With 6 mm seeds gone, neither can eat them; the specialist loses its main food.
The specialist eats almost nothing above about 9 mm.
Right: the specialist depends on 6 mm food; the generalist uses sizes from 0 to 20 mm.

items.q: Where 6 mm seeds are plentiful year after year, the specialist is more common than the generalist. Which explanation fits best?
options: It handles 6 mm seeds more efficiently than the generalist
The generalist is unable to eat 6 mm seeds
Specialists have more offspring in each generation
Generalists avoid areas where seeds are common

why.correct: Specialists can win where conditions are stable and their resource is abundant.
options: Right: specializing often means being better at one task, which pays off when that resource is reliable.
The generalist’s curve includes 6 mm food.
The figure shows food use, not number of offspring.
Nothing in the figure suggests that.

items.q: Which species is the best example of a generalist?
options: A koala that eats the leaves of a few eucalyptus species
A coyote eating rodents, fruit and insects in many places
A caterpillar that feeds on a single kind of milkweed plant
A frog that lives in one cold mountain spring

why.correct: Generalists use many foods and live in many habitats.
options: One kind of food is a narrow niche: a specialist.
Right: many foods and many habitats make a broad niche.
One host plant is a narrow niche: a specialist.
One small habitat is a narrow niche.

items.q: Why are specialist species more likely than generalists to decline when a habitat changes?
options: They reproduce faster and use up their food
They are smaller and weaker than most generalists
They rely on few resources, with little to switch to
They are eaten by generalists in disturbed areas

why.correct: A narrow niche means fewer options when conditions change.
options: How fast they reproduce is not what makes a species a specialist.
Body size does not define a specialist; pandas are large.
Right: if their resource declines, they have no fallback.
Predation can happen, but the main reason is their narrow niche.

items.q: Explain why rats, a generalist species, often increase when a forest is replaced by a city.

why.correct: Broad niche, so new foods and shelters can be used, so the population grows.

specific.frame: Rats ___, so in a city they ___, which ___.

cause.label: Niche
options: eat many foods and use many kinds of shelter
eat one kind of forest seed
live only in tree holes

why.1: One kind of food would describe a specialist.
why.2: One kind of shelter would describe a specialist.

effect.label: What they find
options: can use garbage, stored food and buildings
lose their only food source
must leave to find forest

why.1: Generalists have no single food source to lose.
why.2: Rats can live in buildings, so they do not need forest.

mechanism.label: Result
options: lets more rats survive and reproduce, so their population increases
lowers the number of young rats
keeps the rat population the same

why.1: More food and shelter means more young survive, not fewer.
why.2: New food and shelter change the population; it grows.

specific.model: Rats eat many foods and use many kinds of shelter, so in a city they can use garbage, stored food and buildings, which lets more rats survive and reproduce, so their population increases.

items.q: Which traits describe a specialist species? Select all that apply.
options: It eats one or a few kinds of food
It tolerates a narrow range of conditions
It lives in many different habitats
It easily spreads into towns and farms

why.correct: Specialists have narrow niches in diet, habitat or conditions.
options: Right: a narrow diet is a narrow niche.
Right: a narrow range of tolerance is part of a narrow niche.
Many habitats describe a generalist.
Spreading into disturbed places is typical of generalists.

items.q: Monarch butterfly caterpillars feed on milkweed plants, and few other plants. Farm weed control has removed much of the milkweed from field edges. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Monarchs switch to eating crops in the fields
Monarch numbers rise because weed control kills their predators
There is no change, because adult butterflies drink nectar
Fewer caterpillars survive, so monarch numbers fall

why.correct: A specialist at any life stage is vulnerable when its key resource is removed.
options: Specialist caterpillars do not switch to a different food plant.
Removing milkweed removes their food; that outweighs any change in predators.
Adults can feed on many flowers, but the caterpillars need milkweed to grow.
Right: as specialists, the caterpillars lose their food plant and cannot switch.

items.q: A land manager wants to protect a specialist beetle that lives in old trees. Which action best fits the beetle’s niche?
options: Leave old and dead trees standing in the managed forest
Plant a mix of fast-growing young trees across the area
Put out bird feeders to give the beetle extra food
Remove dead wood so the forest looks tidier

why.correct: Protecting a specialist means protecting its specific resource.
options: Right: it protects the narrow resource the beetle depends on.
Young trees do not provide the old-tree habitat the specialist needs.
Bird feeders do not supply the beetle’s food or habitat.
That removes the very resource the specialist needs.

items.q: Cockroaches live in kitchens, sewers, forests and caves, and eat almost any plant or animal matter. Which statement best predicts how they respond to a city growing into nearby woods?
options: They decline because their single food plant is cut down
They spread into the new buildings and do well
They move deeper into the remaining woods to avoid buildings
They stop reproducing until the woods grow back

why.correct: Generalists often thrive in changed and human-made places.
options: Cockroaches have no single food plant; they eat almost anything.
Right: as generalists, they can use the food and shelter of a city.
Generalists do not need to avoid buildings; many live in them.
Nothing about their niche ties breeding to woods.

items.q: Two lizard species live on the same island. One eats only ants; the other eats ants, beetles, spiders and fruit. A disease kills most of the island’s ants. Which lizard population is more likely to recover, and why?
options: The ant eater, because it is more efficient at catching ants
Both equally, because both eat ants
The one with the broad diet, because it can eat other foods
Neither, because the disease kills the lizards too

why.correct: When one resource collapses, the species with alternatives recovers.
options: Efficiency does not help when the ants are gone.
Only one has other foods to switch to.
Right: the generalist switches to beetles, spiders and fruit.
The disease kills ants; nothing says it affects lizards.
